slides.say: n is a positive odd number. The product n, times n plus two, times n plus four, is necessarily divisible by:

So n is positive and odd. n, n plus two and n plus four are three odd numbers in a row, and we multiply them. What number is the product always divisible by? [short pause] We'll start with one group and check the choices. If several choices remain, we'll choose another group that helps separate them. Then we'll explain why the answer always works.
at: three odd numbers in a row

slides.say: [short pause] Let's start by plugging in numbers, with the smallest group, one, three and five. One times three times five is fifteen. Fifteen is not divisible by forty-five, so choice number one is out.
But fifteen is divisible by fifteen, five and three. So all three of those choices still work for this example. We need another group to tell them apart.

Now we need a second group, and we have to choose it carefully. Take three, five and seven. Five is in the multiplication, and so is three. So the product is divisible by fifteen, and it can't rule out fifteen. Five, seven and nine has the same problem. So we need a group with no multiple of five.
at: So the product is divisible by fifteen

slides.say: Let's choose seven, nine and eleven. To check five, we only need the last digit of the product, because a number is divisible by five only when it ends in zero or five. The last digit of a product comes only from the last digits. Seven times nine is sixty-three, which ends in three. Times eleven, it still ends in three, because three times one is three.

A number that ends in three isn't divisible by five. So it isn't divisible by fifteen either, because fifteen is five times three. Choice numbers two and four are out. Only three is left, and choice number three is our answer.
at: So it isn't divisible by fifteen
choice number three is our answer

slides.say: Now by understanding. Why is the product always divisible by three? Let's write the odd numbers in a row: one, three, five, seven, nine, eleven, thirteen, fifteen. Three, nine and fifteen are divisible by three. Why every third odd number? Multiples of three go three, six, nine, twelve, fifteen. They alternate odd and even. So the odd multiples are six apart. The odd numbers go up by two, so six is three steps along that list. Every three odd numbers in a row therefore include a multiple of three.
at: Three, nine and fifteen are divisible
Every three odd numbers in a row

slides.say: Seven, nine and eleven include nine. Eleven, thirteen and fifteen include fifteen. So one number in the multiplication is divisible by three, and the whole product is divisible by three too. Choice number three is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
